profiles.meeting_scenario: A design review meeting in a clinical pharmacometrics group at a university-affiliated cancer center reviewing the near-final internal tutorial 'Using $DESIGN in NONMEM for Clinical Trial Evaluation and Optimization.' The tutorial is slated for a methods workshop for pharmacometrics fellows, trial statisticians, and clinical pharmacology scientists who already build NONMEM estimation models but have limited experience with trial design evaluation. The agenda is to decide whether the full draft is ready for pilot release, verify that the simple and complex worked examples are pitched appropriately, confirm how the full draft should frame expected precision and identifiability via the Fisher Information Matrix, and settle how clearly the document should direct readers to PopED or PFIM 4.0 for more elaborate designs. The expected outcome is conditional approval of the full draft with a short list of wording and structural edits before the workshop.

members.name: Dr. Elena Markovic
members.expertise: Population PK/PD modeling, NONMEM implementation, model-informed early-phase trial design
members.background: A physician-scientist who leads the center's pharmacometrics methods group and has built internal training modules to help clinical teams stay within familiar NONMEM workflows whenever possible.
members.private_state: She wants the full draft approved with minimal restructuring because the workshop materials are already scheduled, and she wants a practical tutorial that shows NONMEM can cover most everyday design-review questions without sending learners into separate software too early.
hidden_assumptions: A tutorial is 'ready' for pilot release if the scientific framing is sound, the example control streams run cleanly on the internal setup, and any nuanced caveats can be delivered verbally during the workshop.

The 'complex example' naturally means the current continuous-data PK/PD example with multiple design groups, optimized sample times, and subject allocation, because that is the advanced case most users will realistically attempt first.

When the full draft discusses 'parameter precision,' it is sufficient to present expected relative standard errors from an invertible expected FIM under the assumed model, with practical caveats mentioned briefly rather than operationalized.
The retrospective section belongs inside the full draft's main body because it uses the same $DESIGN machinery and will be read by the same audience as part of one coherent tutorial.
Providing 'clear guidance' means concise wording, a short limitations box, and perhaps a spoken reminder that noncontinuous or elaborate designs may need PopED or PFIM.

members.name: Dr. Samuel Reed
members.role: Senior Biostatistician and Trial Design Methodology Reviewer
members.expertise: Optimal design evaluation, trial operating characteristics, statistical review of model-based design guidance
members.background: A biostatistician who supports first-in-human and proof-of-concept protocols and routinely reviews whether internal methods documents are precise enough to be reused without the original instructor present.
members.private_state: He wants the tutorial to be methodologically defensible when circulated beyond the workshop and is particularly concerned that readers may overgeneralize FIM-based results or miss the practical boundary between a convenient NONMEM demonstration and a recommendation fit for design decisions.
hidden_assumptions: A tutorial is 'ready' only if the written document itself is self-sufficient enough that a reader can reuse it later without relying on workshop commentary to avoid misleading conclusions.

The 'complex example' should expose where the comfortable NONMEM $DESIGN use case ends, so that advanced readers do not mistake technical sophistication within continuous PK/PD models for coverage of harder design classes.
Claims about 'parameter precision' need to be explicitly framed as expected precision under the assumed model and separated from broader claims about practical estimability in finite samples.

When reviewing the full draft, the main approval target is the prospective trial evaluation and optimization workflow; retrospective FIM assessment is acceptable only if clearly demarcated as a secondary use case within the same document.
Providing 'clear guidance' means explicit written decision support—such as a short rule set or trigger list—for when users should remain in NONMEM versus move to PopED or PFIM.

misalignment_points.topic: What counts as 'ready' for pilot release
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both say the full draft should be 'ready' for the workshop pilot.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the full draft is ready if the examples execute, the core scientific message is correct, and finer cautions can be handled live during the session.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means the full draft is ready only if the document itself is sufficiently self-contained to prevent overinterpretation of FIM outputs when reused later without live explanation.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: In internal design reviews, 'ready' is a routine release word that usually goes unexamined; both assume they are applying the normal institutional standard, so the different threshold stays latent.

misalignment_points.surface_form: Both refer approvingly to keeping 'one simple and one complex example' in the tutorial.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means the existing complex example: a continuous-data PK/PD design with multiple groups, optimized sampling times, dose settings, and subject allocation handled end-to-end in NONMEM.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means an example that makes methodological boundary conditions visible, such as showing that more elaborate trial structures or noncontinuous endpoints fall outside the comfortable $DESIGN use case.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: The phrase 'complex example' feels like ordinary pedagogic shorthand, and both sincerely think they are endorsing an advanced second example, so neither notices they are classifying different kinds of complexity.

misalignment_points.topic: Boundary of what the 'full draft' covers for approval
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both discuss whether the point belongs in 'the full draft' or 'the complete document.'
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 treats the retrospective use of $DESIGN on an existing model-plus-dataset combination as part of the same core tutorial package being approved today.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 treats the complete document's primary reviewed scope as the prospective design-evaluation workflow, with retrospective uncertainty assessment included only if clearly separated as ancillary material within the full draft.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: Because the retrospective section is already inside the same file and uses the same terminology and software feature, both can naturally talk about 'the full draft' while silently drawing different boundaries around its main approved content.

misalignment_points.topic: What it means to provide 'clear guidance'
misalignment_points.surface_form: Both agree the tutorial should provide 'clear guidance' on limitations and when to use PopED or PFIM.
misalignment_points.member_a_understanding: M1 means clear guidance can be delivered through concise prose, a brief boxed caution, and workshop narration that keeps the document lightweight.
misalignment_points.member_b_understanding: M2 means clear guidance should be explicit and operational in writing, such as a short checklist or rule-based trigger for when NONMEM $DESIGN is only illustrative versus when dedicated software is needed.
misalignment_points.why_undetected: They fully agree on the need for guidance and on the destination tools, so the hidden difference is only in how explicit the written mechanism should be; that procedural distinction is easy to overlook in a cooperative review.

turns.inner_thought: I need this to clear today with only light edits. The workshop materials are already timed out, the NONMEM examples run cleanly on our internal setup, and the framing is scientifically fine. For a pilot, that is ready. Any finer cautions can be handled in the room. I also want to keep the retrospective piece inside the same package and avoid turning the handout into a long decision manual about when to leave NONMEM.
turns.utterance: Thanks for joining. What I want to settle today is whether the full draft is ready for the workshop pilot, and then do one last pass on the examples and the guidance language before we freeze it.

turns.inner_thought: It's close, but ready means the document can stand on its own later, not just work with Elena talking over the slides. These things get reused. turns.utterance: Overall, the complete document is in good shape. My main check is whether, once it's in circulation, it still gives readers clear guidance and enough written framing to stand on its own.

turns.inner_thought: Now the precision language. This has to say explicitly that FIM-based quantities are expected under the assumed model, not a claim about what will be estimable in finite samples. turns.inner_thought: I still need more than a cautionary tone. The tutorial should give written decision support: at least a short trigger list for when the comfortable continuous-data NONMEM template stops being the right one and users should move to PopED or PFIM.
